title: Reverse a string (convert to char array, swap from both ends, or use StringBuilder.reverse()).

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in opposite order. Because String is immutable you cannot reverse it in place; you either convert to a `char[]` and swap with two pointers, or you use `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`. Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, since a new sequence of characters must be created.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India generates a reversed reference code from a transaction id for a simple checksum. Rajesh's id "TXN123" becomes "321NXT". A clerk writes the characters out backwards onto a new slip, because the original id slip cannot be rewritten.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build a new string with the characters flipped — swap from both ends of a char array, or use StringBuilder.reverse().
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in opposite order. Because String is immutable you cannot reverse it in place; you either convert to a `char[]` and swap with two pointers, or you use `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`. Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, since a new sequence of characters must be created.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India generates a reversed reference code from a transaction id for a simple checksum. Rajesh's id "TXN123" becomes "321NXT". A clerk writes the characters out backwards onto a new slip, because the original id slip cannot be rewritten.

**One line to remember:** Build a new string with the characters flipped — swap from both ends of a char array, or use StringBuilder.reverse().

sections.s2_technical:
The simplest professional approach is `new StringBuilder(original).reverse().toString()`. StringBuilder is a mutable character buffer, so its `reverse` method flips the characters in place inside the builder, and then `toString` produces the final String. This is concise and correct.

The manual approach shows you understand the mechanics. You call `original.toCharArray()` to get a mutable `char[]`, then use two pointers: `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. You swap `chars[left]` and `chars[right]`, move inward, and continue while `left < right`. Finally `new String(chars)` builds the reversed String. This mirrors the array-reversal two-pointer technique.

Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, because the original String is immutable so a new character sequence must be allocated. A senior nuance is Unicode: a single visible character can be composed of a surrogate pair of two chars, and naive char-by-char reversal can corrupt such characters. StringBuilder.reverse handles surrogate pairs correctly, which is one reason to prefer it in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India derives a short reversed reference from a transaction id for a lightweight verification code printed on Rajesh's receipt. The system takes the id and produces its reverse. This is exactly how string reversal works — flip the characters into a new string.

Problem 2 — Because a String cannot be changed in place, we cannot just rearrange the original; we must build a new string. This is exactly why we convert to a char array or use StringBuilder, both of which create a fresh character sequence.

The code has a `ReferenceGenerator` class with two methods: `reverseManual` using a char array and two pointers, and `reverseBuiltIn` using StringBuilder. The demo reverses a transaction id with both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: `txnId = "TXN123"`.

Step 1 — `reverseManual` converts to char array `['T','X','N','1','2','3']`, with `left=0`, `right=5`.

Step 2 — Swap index 0 and 5: `['3','X','N','1','2','T']`. Move to `left=1`, `right=4`.

Step 3 — Swap index 1 and 4: `['3','2','N','1','X','T']`. Move to `left=2`, `right=3`.

Step 4 — Swap index 2 and 3: `['3','2','1','N','X','T']`. Move to `left=3`, `right=2`, loop stops.

Step 5 — Build new String `"321NXT"` and return it.

Step 6 — `reverseBuiltIn` produces the same `"321NXT"` via StringBuilder. Both are logged.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Original txn id:        TXN123
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Reversed (two-pointer): 321NXT
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Reversed (StringBuilder): 321NXT
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in the opposite order. Because a String in Java is immutable, I cannot reverse it in place, so I must create a new sequence of characters. The clean production approach is to wrap the string in a StringBuilder, call its reverse method, and convert back to a String. The manual approach, which shows I understand the mechanics, is to convert the string to a character array and use two pointers, one from each end, swapping and moving inward until they meet, then build a new string from the array. Both approaches are linear time and linear space because a new character sequence has to be allocated.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used string reversal to generate a lightweight verification reference from a transaction id, printed on the customer's receipt. Rajesh's transaction id becomes its reverse as a simple checksum-style code.

The nuance I raise in an interview is Unicode correctness. A single visible character can be made of a surrogate pair of two underlying char values, and a naive character-by-character reversal can split and corrupt that pair. The StringBuilder reverse method is aware of surrogate pairs and keeps them intact, which is why I prefer it in production over hand-rolled reversal when the input might contain characters beyond the basic range.
